name: Confirmation Bias
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Seeing What You Already Believe: Confirmation Bias in Crypto Markets
lesson.summary: Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek out, favor, and remember information that supports what a person already believes, and it is a major reason blockchain hype cycles can persist long after warning signs accumulate.
lesson.body:
Confirmation bias is the well documented tendency for people to search for, interpret, and recall information in ways that confirm beliefs they already hold, while discounting or simply not noticing information that contradicts those beliefs. It is not a flaw limited to careless thinkers; it operates on experts and novices alike, because it happens at the level of what information gets attention and how it gets interpreted, not at the level of intelligence or effort. In blockchain markets, confirmation bias has an unusually clean environment to operate in, because the space produces a constant, high volume stream of both bullish and bearish information, giving anyone motivated to find support for either view plenty of raw material to select from.

An investor who has already bought into a token tends to follow accounts, communities, and news sources that reliably produce optimistic takes: a partnership announcement, a rising active address count, a comparison to an earlier token that returned enormous gains. The same investor tends to scroll past, or actively argue against, a critical analysis of the same project's token economics, treating a well reasoned bear case as noise from someone who does not understand the technology, rather than as evidence worth weighing. This is not simple stubbornness; it is confirmation bias doing exactly what it does, filtering the incoming stream of information along the axis of does this support what I already own rather than the axis of is this actually true.

Confirmation bias interacts dangerously with sunk cost. Once money is committed, the psychological cost of concluding the investment was a mistake rises, which increases the pull toward information that avoids that conclusion. This produces a recognizable pattern across many blockchain boom and bust cycles: as a project's fundamentals visibly deteriorate, its most invested community members frequently become more vocal in their certainty, not less, because the community itself increasingly filters toward voices that confirm continued belief and away from voices that do not.

The practical defense against confirmation bias is not simply trying harder to be open minded, since the bias operates below the level most people can consciously monitor in themselves. A more reliable defense is structural: deliberately seeking out the strongest available counterargument to a position before investing, tracking a small number of specific, falsifiable predictions rather than a vague overall sentiment, and treating a claim's popularity within a community someone already belongs to as irrelevant to whether it is true. That last discipline turns out to matter especially in blockchain markets, where confirmation bias rarely operates alone; it is very often reinforced by a second, related bias covered next, the tendency to believe something is more likely to be right simply because many other people appear to believe it too.
